title: Idioms and proverbs
intro: Turkish speech is full of idioms (*deyimler*), proverbs (*atasözleri*) and similes (*benzetmeler*). Many idioms rest on a part of the body: *göz kulak olmak*, to keep an eye on something, is literally to be eye and ear to it. This unit gathers the most useful ones, shows which parts of an idiom can change and which are frozen, and how speakers slip a proverb into a conversation.

sections.title: Göz kulak olmak: idioms of the body

blocks.text: An idiom (*deyim*) is a fixed group of words whose meaning is more than the sum of its parts. Parts of the body supply hundreds of them: TDK's dictionary lists dozens under *göz* alone. Most are verb phrases: a body part, often with a possessive or a case ending, and a verb. Learn each one whole, with the case its object takes: *çocuklara göz kulak olmak* (dative), *birinin sözüne kulak asmamak* (dative), *bir işle başa çıkmak* (with `-(y)lA`).

blocks.caption: Seven parts of the body, three idioms each
head: Idiom
Word for word
Meaning
rows: to keep an eye on, to look after (+ dative)
to like, to take to (someone or something)
to be overlooked, to slip past
to do what comes from one's hand
to take no notice of (+ dative)
to let it escape from one's mouth
to grin from ear to ear
to happen to someone (usually something bad)
to come out at the head
to indulge, to give too much leeway (+ dative)
to be nice to someone's face, and not behind their back
to turn one's nose up at (+ dative)
to be badly missed (the thing missed is the subject)

blocks.text: **The picture is not a hint.** Some idioms are transparent (*el ele vermek*), others not at all (*burnunda tütmek*: a smell of home that won't leave you). Don't guess a meaning from the parts, and don't swap a word for a synonym: *göz atmak* (to glance at) works, *göz fırlatmak* doesn't.

items.tr: Ben yokken çocuklara göz kulak olur musun?
items.seg: Ben yok|ken çocuk|lar|a göz kulak ol|ur mu|sun?
items.en: Will you keep an eye on the children while I'm out?

items.tr: Bu hata nasıl gözümüzden kaçtı?
items.seg: Bu hata nasıl göz|ümüz|den kaç|tı?
items.en: How did we miss this mistake?

items.tr: Sürprizi ağzından kaçırdı.
items.seg: Sürpriz|i ağz|ı|n|dan kaçır|dı.
items.en: He let the surprise slip.

items.tr: Elimden geleni yapacağım, söz veriyorum.
items.seg: El|im|den gel|en|i yap|acağ|ım, söz ver|iyor|um.
items.en: I'll do my best, I promise.

items.tr: Babam benim sözlerime hiç kulak asmaz.
items.seg: Baba|m ben|im söz|ler|im|e hiç kulak as|maz.
items.en: My father never takes any notice of what I say.

items.tr: Annemin yemekleri burnumda tütüyor.
items.seg: Anne|m|in yemek|ler|i burn|um|da tüt|üyor.
items.en: I really miss my mother's cooking.
items.note: The cooking is the subject; the possessive on *burun* says who misses it.

blocks.text: *Göz kulak olmak* is **to keep an eye on**; *göz koymak* is **to have your eye on** something that isn't yours, to covet it: *Komşunun bahçesine göz koymuş* (he has his eye on the neighbour's garden).
English has body idioms too, often with another part or picture: *ağzından kaçırmak* is to let the cat out of the bag, *kulak vermek* to lend an ear, *yüzü kızarmak* to go red in the face.

A proverb (*atasözü*, literally a word of the ancestors) is a complete sentence of traditional advice or observation. An idiom is a phrase you fit into your own sentence; a proverb is a sentence you quote whole: *Damlaya damlaya göl olur*, drop by drop a lake forms. Proverbs are anonymous and short, and they speak of everyone and no one in particular, which shapes their grammar.

blocks.label: Four shapes
lines: no verb          Kız beşikte, çeyiz sandıkta.

blocks.text: **The aorist** states what is always true ([A2 unit 4](gp-aorist-uses)): *Dost kara günde belli olur*, a friend shows himself on a dark day. **A `-(y)An` participle** names whoever does something ([B1 unit 5](gp-headless-an)): *Gülü seven dikenine katlanır*, whoever loves the rose puts up with its thorns. **The imperative** speaks to every listener at once ([A1 unit 12](gp-imperative)): *Ayağını yorganına göre uzat*, stretch your legs only as far as your quilt goes. Some proverbs have no verb at all, or only `-DIr` ([B2 unit 5](gp-dir-formal)): *Kız beşikte, çeyiz sandıkta*; *Komşu komşunun külüne muhtaçtır*.

rows: Drop by drop, it becomes a lake.

A friend shows on a black day.
A friend in need is a friend indeed.
A real friend tells you unwelcome truths.
A grape darkens by looking at a grape.
People take on the ways of those around them.
Whoever loves the rose puts up with its thorn.

Sütten ağzı yanan yoğurdu üfleyerek yer.

Stretch your feet according to your quilt.
A neighbour needs a neighbour's ashes.
The girl in the cradle, the trousseau in the chest.

My daughter, I'm telling you; my daughter-in-law, you understand.
Criticizing someone indirectly, by talking to someone else.

blocks.text: **Using a proverb.** Speakers drop a proverb at the end of a story to sum it up, often with a frame: *Ne demişler?* (What do they say?), *Atalarımız ne demiş:* (as our ancestors said), *Boşuna dememişler* (it's not for nothing they say), *derler ya* (as they say). Among people who know it, half a proverb is enough: *Damlaya damlaya…*, *Sütten ağzı yanan…*

items.tr: Her ay biraz para biriktiriyorum; damlaya damlaya göl olur.
items.seg: Her ay biraz para biriktir|iyor|um; damla|y|a damla|y|a göl ol|ur.
items.en: I save a little money every month; it all adds up.

items.tr: Boşuna dememişler: dost kara günde belli olur.
items.seg: Boşuna de|me|miş|ler: dost kara gün|de belli ol|ur.
items.en: It's not for nothing they say a friend in need is a friend indeed.

items.tr: Ne demişler? Acele işe şeytan karışır. Bir daha kontrol et.
items.seg: Ne de|miş|ler? Acele iş|e şeytan karış|ır. Bir daha kontrol et.
items.en: What do they say? Haste makes waste. Check it again.

items.tr: Ateş olmayan yerden duman çıkmaz; bu söylentide bir gerçek payı olmalı.
items.seg: Ateş ol|ma|y|an yer|den duman çık|maz; bu söylenti|de bir gerçek pay|ı ol|malı.
items.en: There's no smoke without fire; there must be some truth in this rumour.

items.tr: Sütten ağzı yanan yoğurdu üfleyerek yer: bir kez kandırıldı, artık kimseye inanmıyor.
items.seg: Süt|ten ağz|ı yan|an yoğurd|u üfle|y|erek ye|r: bir kez kandır|ıl|dı, artık kimse|y|e inan|mı|yor.
items.en: Once bitten, twice shy: he was fooled once, and now he believes nobody.

blocks.text: A proverb states what is always true. To apply it to one person, step back into ordinary tenses: *Gülü seven dikenine katlanır* becomes *Onu seviyorsan huyuna da katlanacaksın* (if you love him, you'll put up with his temper too).
Proverbs carry the authority of the elders. Used to round off a story, one adds a smile; aimed at someone's mistake, it can sound like a lecture.

Some proverbs have exact English twins (*Ateş olmayan yerden duman çıkmaz*, no smoke without fire); others share the idea in another picture (*Ayağını yorganına göre uzat*, cut your coat according to your cloth). Learn the Turkish picture: it is what a Turkish listener hears.

sections.title: Gözüm yemedi: what changes inside an idiom

blocks.text: An idiom is frozen, but not completely. Two things change freely: the possessive on the body part, which follows the person concerned, and the tense and person of the verb. Everything else stays: the words themselves, the case endings, and often the polarity.

**Who is the subject?** In many idioms the grammatical subject is the body part, not the person. The verb then stays in the third person, and only the possessive changes: *Gözüm yemedi* (I didn't dare: my eye didn't eat), *Başımız göğe erdi* (we were overjoyed), *Yüzün kızardı* (you blushed).

rows.en: I was grinning from ear to ear
you were grinning from ear to ear
he or she was grinning from ear to ear
we were grinning from ear to ear
you were grinning from ear to ear (plural or polite)
they were grinning from ear to ear

blocks.text: In other idioms the person is the subject, and the body part is frozen with no possessive at all: *Bu işle başa çıkamadık* (we couldn't cope with this job), *Çocuklara göz kulak ol* (keep an eye on the children), *Öğretmenine kulak ver* (listen to your teacher).

head: Idiom
What changes
Example
rows: the possessive on göz; the thing missed is the subject
the possessive on burun; the thing missed is the subject
the person of the verb; baş never changes

blocks.text: **Frozen polarity.** Some idioms live in the negative: *gözü yememek* (not to dare), *el sürmemek* (not to touch something at all), *kulak asmamak* (to take no notice), *yüzüne bakmamak* (to ignore someone). Dictionaries may list a positive form, but in speech you hear the negative, or a question that expects one: *Kimse pastaya el sürmedi mi?*

**Frozen wishes.** Set phrases keep the form they were born with, and only the possessive follows the listener: *Gözün aydın* (congratulations, to someone with happy news such as a birth or a homecoming; literally, your eye is bright), *Darısı başına* (may the same good luck come to you; at a wedding, said to the unmarried; literally, its millet on your head), *Ağzına sağlık* (well said; literally, health to your mouth). To several people, or politely: *Gözünüz aydın*, *Darısı başınıza*, *Ağzınıza sağlık*. *Kulağına küpe olsun* (let it be a lesson to you: an earring in your ear) keeps the third-person imperative of [A2 unit 7](gp-imperative-3rd); told afterwards, it becomes a plain past: *Bu olay kulağıma küpe oldu*.

**Literal or idiomatic?** Many idioms keep a literal reading, and the context decides: *Ağzı açık kaldı* (his mouth stayed open, or: he was stunned), *kına yakmak* (to apply henna, or: to rejoice at someone's misfortune: *Ben gidince arkamdan kına yakmışlar*, apparently they celebrated when I left).

items.en: I didn't dare to jump into the sea.

items.seg: Bu olay kulağ|ım|a küpe ol|du.

items.seg: Abla|n|ın bebeğ|i ol|muş, göz|ün aydın!
items.en: I hear your sister has had her baby, congratulations!

items.seg: Düğün|den sonra biz|e “Darı|s|ı baş|ınız|a!” de|di|ler.
items.en: After the wedding they said to us, “May you be next!”

items.tr: Yemeğine hiç el sürmedi; bir şey mi oldu?
items.seg: Yemeğ|i|n|e hiç el sür|me|di; bir şey mi ol|du?
items.en: She didn't touch her food at all; has something happened?

items.tr: Bu işle tek başımıza başa çıkamayız.
items.seg: Bu iş|le tek baş|ımız|a baş|a çık|a|ma|y|ız.

blocks.text: Don't move the possessive to the person: *Gözüm yemedi*, not *Ben gözümü yemedim*. And keep the case the idiom wants: *çocuklara göz kulak olmak*, never *çocukları göz kulak olmak*.

sections.title: Buz gibi, kuzu gibi: similes with gibi

blocks.text: A simile (*benzetme*) compares with *gibi* (like, [A2 unit 8](gp-equative)). A few dozen are fixed, and Turkish speakers use them all the time, often as plain intensifiers: *buz gibi* is not so much **like ice** as **ice-cold**.

head: Simile
Word for word
Meaning
rows: ice-cold; cold and distant (of a look or a manner)
very sweet; perfectly well, without a doubt
fluently (su gibi okumak, su gibi bilmek); freely (para su gibi gidiyor)
to get by like a rose
to get along beautifully; to live comfortably

blocks.text: **Two positions.** Before a noun, the simile works as an adjective: *buz gibi su* (ice-cold water), *kar gibi çarşaflar* (snow-white sheets). After the subject, it describes it or how something is done: *Dedem turp gibi* (Grandpa is fit as a fiddle), *Çocuklar kuzu gibi oturdu* (the children sat as good as gold). Some can take the adjective they stand for: *buz gibi soğuk*, *kar gibi beyaz*, *pamuk gibi yumuşak*.

**Intensifiers.** *Bal gibi* and *buz gibi* can also simply mean **certainly**: *Bal gibi biliyorsun* (you know perfectly well), *Bu bal gibi yalan* (this is a lie, plain and simple). With a pronoun, *gibi* takes the genitive, as you know: *senin gibi*, *onun gibi*.

**Similes in one word.** `-cAsInA` ([B2 unit 2](gp-cesine)) and the intensive reduplication of [A2 unit 8](gp-intensive-reduplication) do similar work inside a single word: *delicesine* (madly), *bembeyaz* (snow-white), *kapkara* (pitch-black).

items.tr: Buz gibi bir su içmek istiyorum.
items.seg: Buz gibi bir su iç|mek ist|iyor|um.
items.en: I'd love a glass of ice-cold water.

items.tr: Düğünde çocuklar kuzu gibi oturdu.
items.seg: Düğün|de çocuk|lar kuzu gibi otur|du.
items.en: At the wedding the children sat as good as gold.

items.tr: Dedem seksen yaşında ama turp gibi.
items.seg: Dede|m seksen yaş|ı|n|da ama turp gibi.
items.en: My grandfather is eighty, but he's fit as a fiddle.

items.tr: Şiiri su gibi okudu, hiç takılmadı.
items.seg: Şiir|i su gibi oku|du, hiç takıl|ma|dı.
items.en: She read the poem fluently, without stumbling once.

items.tr: Bal gibi biliyorsun, neden soruyorsun?
items.seg: Bal gibi bil|iyor|sun, neden sor|uyor|sun?
items.en: You know perfectly well, so why are you asking?

items.tr: Kayınvalidesiyle gül gibi geçiniyor.
items.seg: Kayınvalide|s|i|y|le gül gibi geçin|iyor.
items.en: She gets along beautifully with her mother-in-law.

items.tr: Tatilde para su gibi gitti.
items.seg: Tatil|de para su gibi git|ti.
items.en: On holiday the money just poured away.

blocks.text: These similes belong to everyday speech; *bal gibi* and *deli gibi* in particular sound casual. In a formal text, say *çok soğuk*, *akıcı bir şekilde*, *kesinlikle*.
English similes usually need **as … as**: as cold as ice, as meek as a lamb. Turkish keeps just the noun and *gibi*, and the adjective is optional.

summary: Body idioms come whole, with the case their object takes: *çocuklara göz kulak olmak*, *sözüne kulak asmamak*, *bir işle başa çıkmak*.
In many idioms the body part is the subject: the verb stays in the third person and the possessive tells you who: *Gözüm yemedi*, *Ağzımız kulaklarımıza vardı*.
Some idioms live in the negative (*gözü yememek*, *el sürmemek*, *kulak asmamak*); set wishes keep their form and change only the possessive (*Gözün aydın*, *Darısı başınıza*).
Proverbs are whole sentences in the aorist (*Damlaya damlaya göl olur*), with a `-(y)An` subject (*Gülü seven dikenine katlanır*), in the imperative (*Ayağını yorganına göre uzat*) or with no verb.
Bring in a proverb with *Ne demişler?* or *Boşuna dememişler*, or say just its first half.
*Gibi* similes work before a noun (*buz gibi su*) or after the subject (*kuzu gibi oturdu*); *bal gibi* and *buz gibi* can simply mean **certainly**.
